prompt: What is Linux's actual relationship to Unix?
hint: Ask what was copied: the code, or the way it behaves.

choices.text: A fork of the Unix source code, taken in 1991
choices.why: No Unix code was taken. That is exactly what could not be done, and the reason the kernel was written from nothing.

choices.text: A reimplementation that copied the interface and none of the code
choices.why: Written from scratch to behave like Unix, which is why it is legally free of it and compatible with it anyway.

choices.text: The same thing under a different name, after the trademark changed hands
choices.why: UNIX is a live trademark with a certification behind it, and Linux does not hold it.

choices.text: A later version of Unix, released by Bell Labs
choices.why: Bell Labs had nothing to do with it. Linux began as one person's project in Helsinki.

prompt: You learn a command on Linux and run it on macOS. POSIX means you can safely assume:
hint: POSIX is a floor. Think about which half of a command line it describes.

choices.text: Very little; the resemblance between the two is superficial
choices.why: Too pessimistic. macOS is a registered UNIX and the core commands genuinely are the same.

choices.text: The command, its flags and the exact text it prints are identical everywhere
choices.why: Output formats and extra flags are precisely where GNU and BSD tools diverge.

choices.text: Whatever runs on one will run unchanged on the other
choices.why: Package managers, service managers and `/proc` have no equivalent, and none of them is POSIX.

choices.text: The command exists and does the same job, though some flags differ
choices.why: The standard fixes the names and the core behaviour, and leaves the extensions above it to each system.

prompt: Which of these carry from a Linux machine to a Mac's Terminal? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate the agreement from what each system built on top of it.

choices.text: `|` sending one program's output into the next
choices.why: Pipes are in the standard and work identically.

choices.text: Paths starting at `/`, with no drive letters
choices.why: One rooted tree is part of the agreement.

choices.text: `apt install` for adding software
choices.why: Package management is not POSIX. macOS has no `apt`.

choices.text: Owner, group and other permission bits
choices.why: The permission model is in the standard.

choices.text: `systemctl` for starting and stopping services
choices.why: systemd is Linux's, and not even every Linux has it. macOS uses launchd.

choices.text: Reading process information out of `/proc`
choices.why: `/proc` is a Linux invention. macOS has no such directory.

prompt: Fill the blank: on Ubuntu, `/bin/sh` is not bash — it is a symbolic link to ___, a smaller and stricter shell.
hint: The section shows the `ls -l` output that says so.

prompt: Match each system to where it actually comes from.
hint: Two of them share an ancestor, one imitated it, and one never met it.

pairs.right: Written from nothing to behave like Unix, sharing no code with it
Descends from BSD, and is a formally registered UNIX
A separate lineage out of VMS, with no Unix ancestry at all
A direct continuation of the Berkeley line

right_distractors: A rewrite of System V commissioned by Bell Labs in the 1980s
A Linux distribution with the kernel replaced

prompt: You type `dcoker ps` and get back `bash: dcoker: command not found`. Which layer is speaking?
hint: The message names itself before the colon.

choices.text: The shell
choices.why: It looked for a program with that name, found none, and said so — and it signed the message `bash:`.

choices.text: The kernel
choices.why: The kernel was never asked. Nothing got as far as being run.

choices.text: Docker, reporting that it did not recognise the subcommand
choices.why: Docker was never reached — and that is the point of reading the prefix.

choices.text: The terminal emulator
choices.why: The terminal drew those characters and has no idea what they mean.

prompt: You run `tty` and it prints `/dev/pts/0`. What is that?
hint: The name is a museum piece. What was a terminal, originally?

choices.text: The file your command's output is being written to
choices.why: Output flows through it, but it is a device rather than a file somebody would open later.

choices.text: A temporary directory the shell uses while it runs
choices.why: Nothing under `/dev` is a scratch directory. It is where devices appear.

choices.text: A pseudo-terminal: the software stand-in for a keyboard and screen
choices.why: Your shell believes it is talking to hardware; it is talking to a window pretending to be some.

choices.text: The physical serial port your terminal is connected to, at the other end of a cable
choices.why: That would be `/dev/ttyS0`. The `pts` form exists precisely because there is no cable.

prompt: You type `zsh` and get a zsh prompt. Now `echo $0` prints `zsh` and `echo $SHELL` prints `/bin/bash`. Why do they disagree?
hint: The two variables answer two different questions.

choices.text: `$SHELL` is stale and will correct itself at the next command
choices.why: It is not stale. It is answering a different question, correctly.

choices.text: One of them reads the full path while the other reads the short name of the very same shell
choices.why: They name two different shells here, not one shell written two ways.

choices.text: zsh failed to start, so bash is still the shell you are typing into
choices.why: `$0` saying `zsh` is the evidence that it did start.

choices.text: `$0` is the shell running now; `$SHELL` is your account's login shell
choices.why: Starting a shell by hand changes what is running and changes nothing about your account.

prompt: Match each symptom to the layer responsible for it.
hint: Ask who would have had to be asked before that message could exist.

pairs.right: The shell — it searched and found no such program
The kernel — it was asked, and it refused

pairs.left: Text in the wrong place, colours stuck on
pairs.right: The terminal emulator — the drawing is confused, not the command

pairs.left: No new prompt, nothing printed, nothing wrong
pairs.right: The program — it is still running and has not finished

right_distractors: The network — the machine has lost its connection
The disk — the filesystem is full and cannot be written to

prompt: Put the shell's loop in order, from the moment you press enter.
items: Expand what you wrote — `*` becomes a list of files, `$HOME` becomes a path
Ask the kernel to run it
trap: The common mistake is putting the expansion after the program is found. It happens first, and that is why `rm *.txt` hands `rm` a list of filenames rather than a `*`.

prompt: Which of these are true of the shell? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section's claim is that it is more ordinary than it looks.

choices.text: It is an ordinary program, with a name and a file
choices.why: Exactly as ordinary as `ls`. Its job just happens to be starting other programs.

choices.text: You can replace it with a different one
choices.why: bash, zsh, dash, fish — the choice is yours and the system does not mind.

choices.text: It is part of the Linux kernel
choices.why: The kernel is the one program in the middle. The shell came from elsewhere entirely.

choices.text: It expands `*` before the command ever sees it
choices.why: Expansion is the shell's step 3, and a great deal of later confusion comes from forgetting it.

choices.text: It has privileges an ordinary program does not
choices.why: None. What it may do is exactly what your user may do.

prompt: Inside a plain `ubuntu` container, `systemctl status` refuses to do anything and mentions PID 1. What is going on?
hint: Consider how much of a computer a container actually starts.

choices.text: The image is damaged, and pulling it again will restore the missing service manager
choices.why: Every plain distribution image behaves this way. Pulling it again changes nothing.

choices.text: systemd is present but stopped, so it has to be started before anything else works
choices.why: There is nothing to start it. PID 1 is whatever you asked the container to run.

choices.text: The machine did not boot, so the service manager it talks to is not running
choices.why: A container runs a single program rather than a whole system. This is its normal state.

choices.text: You are not root inside this environment, so the request is being refused
choices.why: It is not a permission problem; the message says so. Being root changes nothing here.

prompt: Lesson 5 is about services and systemd. Which practice machine will NOT do for it?
hint: One of these never boots.

choices.text: A virtual machine
choices.why: It boots like real hardware, so systemd is there in full.

choices.text: A container
choices.why: No boot, so no init system. Use a virtual machine or WSL for that lesson.

choices.text: A rented cloud instance
choices.why: An ordinary booted machine, and the closest thing to how it will be at work.

choices.text: WSL 2
choices.why: A real kernel, and current versions run systemd.

prompt: What does a machine to practise on have to give you? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three properties, and each one rules out something that looks convenient.

choices.text: You can break it without it being a disaster
choices.why: You will run something destructive by accident, and that has to be survivable.

choices.text: You can throw it away and start clean
choices.why: Starting again is a learning tool, not an admission of failure.

choices.text: It is a real Linux, not a simulation of one
choices.why: The whole subject is how the actual system behaves.

choices.text: It has a graphical desktop installed
choices.why: Most machines you will meet professionally have no desktop at all.

choices.text: It is the same distribution as the one used in the videos
choices.why: Lesson 2 is about the differences. Meeting one early is useful rather than a problem.

prompt: Fill the blank: in `docker run -it ___ ubuntu:24.04 bash`, that flag is what deletes the machine the moment you type `exit`.
hint: It is the one that makes the container a throwaway.

prompt: Why is a Mac's Terminal a poor substitute for a Linux on this course, even though most commands work?
hint: It is in the family — the question is what sits above the agreement.

choices.text: It is a BSD userland: flags differ, and `/proc`, `apt` and systemd are absent
choices.why: Fine for lessons 3 and 4, and actively misleading for 2, 5, 7 and 11.

choices.text: macOS sits outside the Unix family, so very little of what you learn here will carry across
choices.why: The opposite: it is a formally registered UNIX. That is why so much does work.

choices.text: Terminal is an emulator rather than a shell, so it runs a simulation of the commands
choices.why: Every terminal is an emulator, including the one on a Linux machine. It runs a real shell.

choices.text: Becoming root on a Mac requires a developer account from Apple
choices.why: `sudo` works there as it does anywhere. That is not the difference.

prompt: A prompt ends in `#` instead of `$`. What does that tell you?
hint: It is about which account the commands will run as.

choices.text: The machine is waiting for you to confirm something
choices.why: A prompt waits for a command, not for a confirmation. It has no question pending.

choices.text: The shell is a different program from bash
choices.why: The character is about privilege, not about which shell you are in.

choices.text: You are root, and what you type has no restrictions
choices.why: Read the last character before pressing enter on anything destructive.

choices.text: The previous command failed and left an error behind
choices.why: A failed command changes the exit status, and leaves the prompt exactly as it was.

prompt: The prompt reads `ana@vm:~/notes$`. What will `pwd` print?
hint: The prompt is writing one of those two forms short.

choices.text: /home/ana/notes
choices.why: `~` is the home directory written short, so the two agree — they are reading the same fact.

choices.text: ~/notes
choices.why: `pwd` prints the path in full. The shortening belongs to the prompt.

choices.text: /notes
choices.why: That would be a directory at the root of the tree, which is somewhere else entirely.

choices.text: notes
choices.why: `pwd` answers with a path from the root, not with the name of the directory you are in.

prompt: Fill the blank: the prompt is a string held in a shell variable called ___.
hint: The section prints it with `echo`.

prompt: Match each piece of `ana@vm:~$` to the question it answers.
hint: Four pieces, four different questions.

pairs.right: Who you are on this machine
Which machine this is
Where you are in the filesystem
Whether you are root

right_distractors: Which shell is reading your line
How long the last command took

prompt: You run a command, and no new prompt appears. What is the honest reading?
hint: A prompt means the shell is ready. Ask what the absence of one means.

choices.text: The terminal has lost its connection to the machine
choices.why: A dropped connection has its own symptoms, and this is not how it looks.

choices.text: The machine has frozen and should be restarted
choices.why: Reaching for the power button here is the expensive mistake this section exists to prevent.

choices.text: It is running; whether it is stuck is a separate question
choices.why: The prompt returns when the command finishes. `ps` and `top` in lesson 6 are how you find out which.

choices.text: The command already finished, without printing anything
choices.why: A command that finishes gives the prompt back, printing or not.

prompt: In `ls -l readme.txt`, which part is the argument?
hint: Three parts: what to run, how to run it, what to run it on.

choices.why: That changes how the command runs, which makes it the option.

choices.text: `readme.txt`
choices.why: The argument is what the command acts on.

choices.text: `ls`
choices.why: That is the command — the program being run.

choices.text: `ls -l`
choices.why: Two parts joined, and the argument is neither of them.

prompt: Which of these are true about options? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what is a rule from what is a habit of one program.

choices.text: `-la` is the same as `-l -a`
choices.why: Combining short options is ordinary, and the order between them rarely matters.

choices.text: A long option is written with two hyphens
choices.why: `--all`, `--recursive`. One hyphen is the short spelling.

choices.text: `-r` and `-R` are the same option written twice
choices.why: Case matters. They are usually two different options.

choices.text: Each short option has a long spelling to match it
choices.why: Which spellings exist is a fact about each program, which is what `man` is for.

choices.text: An option can take a value of its own, as in `-n 2`
choices.why: The `2` belongs to the option — it says how many.

prompt: There is a file named `-strange`, and `ls -strange` answers `invalid option -- 'e'`. Why?
hint: Ask what the program saw, character by character.

choices.text: The filename holds a character `ls` is unable to print on this terminal
choices.why: It printed the name fine a moment earlier. The problem arrived before any printing.

choices.text: The file is missing, and the message is `ls` guessing at what you meant
choices.why: The file is right there. It was never looked for.

choices.text: The directory has to be readable before a name inside it can be used
choices.why: The directory was readable — the plain `ls` had already listed it.

choices.text: Anything starting with `-` is read as options, so the name was never an argument
choices.why: It took the letters one at a time and stopped at the first that is not an `ls` option.

prompt: Fill the blank: writing ___ on its own tells a command that the options have finished and everything after it is an argument.
hint: Two characters, and it is what rescues a file whose name begins with a hyphen.

prompt: `ls with space.txt` prints two errors — one about `with`, one about `space.txt`. Why two?
hint: Ask who broke the line up, and when.

choices.text: The shell split the line on the space, so `ls` was handed two names
choices.why: Quoting it makes it one argument again, which is the fix and the whole lesson.

choices.text: `ls` tried the name, failed, and retried it in two halves
choices.why: It did not retry anything. It was given two names and reported on each.

choices.text: A file name is not allowed to hold a space on Linux
choices.why: It is allowed, and the file exists. The difficulty is in getting the name through the shell intact.

choices.text: The `.txt` on the end was read as a separate argument by itself
choices.why: The split happened at the space, and the extension travelled with the second half.

prompt: Match each message to the part of the command that was wrong.
hint: Ask how far the line got before it failed.

pairs.right: The command — no program by that name
The option — the program ran and refused the flag
The argument — the program looked and found nothing

right_distractors: The terminal — the drawing became confused
The kernel — it refused to run the program at all

prompt: What does `Ctrl+C` do at a terminal?
hint: It is the one key that means something else here.

choices.text: Copies whatever text is selected, as it does elsewhere
choices.why: That is `Ctrl+Shift+C` in most Linux terminals. The shift is what keeps `Ctrl+C` free.

choices.text: Interrupts the command that is running
choices.why: The exit status afterwards is 130, which is the number for interrupted.

choices.text: Closes the terminal window and ends the session
choices.why: That is closer to `Ctrl+D` at an empty prompt, and it means something different again.

choices.text: Pauses the output until you press it a second time
choices.why: Pausing the output is `Ctrl+S`, and `Ctrl+Q` is what resumes it.

prompt: Your terminal stops responding. Nothing you type appears. What should you try first?
hint: There is a key that does exactly this, and people press it by accident reaching for save.

choices.text: Close the window and open a new terminal
choices.why: That throws away the session, and the screen was going to come back on its own.

choices.text: Restart the machine
choices.why: The most expensive answer to the cheapest problem. Nothing was wrong with it.

choices.text: Press `Ctrl+Q`
choices.why: `Ctrl+S` pauses the output and `Ctrl+Q` resumes it. This is the most common false alarm there is.

choices.text: Wait for the running command to finish
choices.why: Waiting works when a command is running. A paused terminal will sit like that for as long as you leave it.

prompt: `cat` with no filename is sitting there reading what you type. Which key ends it properly?
hint: One key interrupts a program; the other says the input is over.

choices.text: `Ctrl+D`, because it says the input has finished
choices.why: An ordinary, successful ending — no `^D` on the screen and no error, just the next prompt.

choices.text: `Ctrl+C`, because it stops the program
choices.why: It does stop it, by interrupting — which throws away what you typed instead of delivering it.

choices.text: `Ctrl+Z`, because it returns you to the prompt
choices.why: That suspends it. You get the prompt back and the program is still there, paused.

choices.text: `Ctrl+L`, because it takes the screen back to a clean state
choices.why: That scrolls the text out of view. The program carries on reading.

prompt: Fill the blank: you press `Ctrl+C`, then run `echo $?`, and the shell prints ___ — the exit status that means the program was interrupted.
hint: The section shows the number in a real session.

prompt: Which of these edit the line you are currently typing? Choose all that apply.
hint: Editing the line is not the same as acting on a running program.

choices.text: `Ctrl+U` — delete back to the start of the line
choices.why: The safest way to abandon a half-typed line: it leaves no doubt about whether anything ran.

choices.text: `Ctrl+A` — jump to the start of the line
choices.why: With `Ctrl+E` for the end, it is how you stop holding the arrow key down.

choices.text: `Ctrl+W` — delete the word before the cursor
choices.why: One word at a time, which is usually the unit you got wrong.

choices.text: `Ctrl+Z` — suspend
choices.why: That acts on a running program, and leaves it paused and alive.

choices.text: `Ctrl+L` — clear the screen
choices.why: The line you are typing survives it. Only the view changes.

prompt: `ls -l /dev/null` prints `crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 1, 3`. Why are there two numbers where a size would be?
hint: A device entry holds no bytes of its own.

choices.text: They are the date and time, in a short format
choices.why: The date appears further along the same line, in its usual format.

choices.text: The major and minor number: which driver, which device
choices.why: The entry points at a driver rather than holding content, so the size column reports that instead.

choices.text: They are how many processes have the device open right now
choices.why: That number never appears in a listing. Lesson 6's `lsof` is what answers it.

choices.text: They are the size, in kilobytes and in blocks
choices.why: A size would take one column, and a device has no size to report.

prompt: `head -3 /proc/meminfo` works, and `head` knows nothing about memory. How?
hint: Ask what the kernel chose to answer in.

choices.text: `head` has a special case for paths beginning with `/proc`
choices.why: It does not. It is the same `head` you use on an ordinary text file.

choices.text: A system service rewrites the file once a second
choices.why: Nothing is written. Its size reads as zero, because no content is stored.

choices.text: The kernel answers in text, in the same shape a file answers in
choices.why: That is the whole agreement, and it is why no tool had to be extended.

choices.text: `/proc` is a database that `head` knows how to query
choices.why: There is no database and no query. There is a stream of text being read.

prompt: Fill the blank: writing to ___ throws the data away, which is why `2> ___` is how you discard a command's errors.
hint: The bin. One path, used twice in that sentence.

prompt: Which of these does the idea genuinely cover? Choose all that apply.
hint: The honest form is 'reached like a file'. Ask what has an owner and a mode.

choices.text: Devices, which appear as entries in `/dev`
choices.why: Opened, read and written like a file, and governed by the same permissions.

choices.text: Kernel state, which appears as text in `/proc`
choices.why: Invented as you look at it, and read by the same tools.

choices.text: TCP connections, which you can read with `cat`
choices.why: You cannot. Internet sockets are not in the filesystem.

choices.text: A process's open files, at `/proc/<pid>/fd`
choices.why: One directory per process, and one entry per descriptor.

prompt: You plug a USB stick into a Linux machine. What does it become?
hint: There is no second tree for it to start.

choices.text: A new drive letter, picked in the order it was found
choices.why: Drive letters are Windows'. There are none here.

choices.text: A directory, somewhere inside the tree that already exists
choices.why: Mounted — and whoever set the machine up chose where.

choices.text: A separate tree, with a root of its own
choices.why: There is one tree. That is the section's whole idea.

choices.text: A file in `/dev`, and that is the whole of it
choices.why: The disk does appear in `/dev`, but it is the mount that makes it navigable.

prompt: Why is `/srv/data/report.csv` a better address than `D:\data\report.csv`?
hint: Ask what happens when the data moves to a bigger disk.

choices.text: It is shorter, and short paths resolve faster
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with it, and resolution is not measurably different.

choices.text: It names no disk, so moving the data breaks no path
choices.why: Which disk is the operator's decision, and no program needs to know.

choices.text: It uses forward slashes, which are more portable between systems
choices.why: The slash helps when writing it, but it is not what makes the address stable.

choices.text: It points at a faster disk, by convention
choices.why: `/srv` is not a convention about speed. It is about what is kept there.

prompt: Fill the blank: attaching a filesystem to a directory so it can be reached is called ___ it.
hint: One verb, and it is the whole idea of the section.

prompt: A backup job writes nightly to `/mnt/backups`, and the disk that should be there fell off a month ago. What has been happening?
hint: An empty mount point is an ordinary directory.

choices.text: The job has been failing every night, with an error
choices.why: It did not fail. The directory exists and is writable, so every write succeeded.

choices.text: The job has been writing to the main disk, complaining about nothing
choices.why: Which is why a backup has to be checked, not only scheduled. Lesson 11 comes back to it.

choices.text: The job has been writing to memory, and losing it at each reboot
choices.why: `/mnt` is not memory. It is an ordinary directory on the main tree.

choices.text: The system has been recreating the mount point each night
choices.why: Nothing recreates a mount by itself. The directory simply stayed there, empty.

prompt: A directory holds `NOTES.TXT`, `Notes.txt` and `notes.txt` at the same time. What does that tell you?
hint: Try the same thing on a Mac and it refuses.

choices.text: The three are links to one file, stored once
choices.why: Links exist and look different in a listing. These are three separate files.

choices.text: `ls` is showing one file three ways
choices.why: : `ls` prints a name once. Three lines are three entries.

choices.text: This filesystem treats upper and lower case as different
choices.why: Which is why a project can work on a Mac and fail on the Linux server that serves it.

choices.text: The directory was created by a program rather than a person
choices.why: Nothing about how it was created changes what names may coexist.

prompt: `file report.pdf` answers `report.pdf: ASCII text`. What happened?
hint: Ask what Linux checked before answering.

choices.text: The PDF is damaged and `file` fell back to a guess
choices.why: Nothing is damaged. There was never a PDF.

choices.text: `file` needs the document to be closed by its program first
choices.why: `file` reads bytes off the disk. Nothing has to be closed.

choices.text: The system associated `.pdf` with a text editor at some point
choices.why: There is no association table. Nothing on the system maps extensions to programs.

choices.text: The name says `.pdf`; the extension decides nothing
choices.why: `file` reads the first bytes and reports what it found, which is the only honest answer.

prompt: Fill the blank: a name beginning with a ___ is left out of an ordinary `ls`, which is the entire mechanism behind a hidden file.
hint: One character. There is no attribute anywhere.

prompt: Which of these are legal in a Linux filename? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two characters are refused. Everything else is allowed, which is not the same as wise.

choices.text: A space
choices.why: Legal, and it is why section 07 spends a page on quoting.

choices.text: A leading hyphen
choices.why: Legal, and the file then needs `--` in front of it for life.

choices.text: A forward slash
choices.why: Refused. It is what separates one directory from the next.

choices.text: A full stop in the middle
choices.why: Ordinary. `archive.tar.gz` has two.

choices.text: An emoji
choices.why: Legal. Advisable is a different question.

prompt: `./windows.sh` answers `cannot execute: required file not found`, and the script is right there. Which file is missing?
hint: A script's first line names a program.

choices.text: A library the script needs, missing from this machine
choices.why: Nothing had got as far as loading a library. The script never started.

choices.text: The interpreter — the shebang reads `/bin/bash` plus a carriage return
choices.why: The kernel looked for a program at that exact path, invisible character included.

choices.text: The script's own directory, which was deleted while it ran
choices.why: The directory is there; `ls` shows the file in it.

choices.text: A temporary file the shell writes before running anything
choices.why: The shell writes no such file. It hands the path to the kernel.

prompt: Of the three faces of a CRLF file, which one costs the most time?
hint: Ask which one gives you no signal at all.

choices.text: The one that runs and prints, with nothing to flag it
choices.why: No error, no clue, and the fault surfaces later somewhere unrelated.

choices.text: `cannot execute: required file not found`
choices.why: Alarming and immediate, which is what makes it cheap to find.

choices.text: `syntax error: unexpected end of file`
choices.why: It names a line that does not exist, and that oddity is itself the clue.

choices.text: The one where `file` reports CRLF line terminators
choices.why: That is the diagnosis, not a failure.

prompt: Fill the blank: run ___ on a script that behaves impossibly, and a CRLF file says so in the last clause of the answer.
hint: One word, four letters, and it reads bytes rather than drawing them.

prompt: Match each symptom to what bash was actually reading.
hint: In each case an invisible byte ended up somewhere it was not expected.

pairs.right: The shebang, read as `/bin/bash` plus a carriage return
`then` and `fi`, each with a carriage return stuck to it

pairs.left: It runs and prints, apparently fine
pairs.right: A value that carries a carriage return along with it

right_distractors: A file whose permissions do not allow it to run
A script written for a shell that is not installed

prompt: Match each directory to what is kept in it.
hint: Four of the eight. One of them is a trap people fall into once.

pairs.right: Configuration for the whole machine, as text
What the machine writes while it runs, logs above all
One directory per person
The administrator's own home directory

right_distractors: The top of the tree, from which everything else hangs
Programs you compiled and installed by hand

prompt: Why can `/etc` be kept in git, and the Windows registry not?
hint: Ask what shape each one is in.

choices.text: Because `/etc` is smaller, and git struggles above a certain size
choices.why: Size is not the difference. Git handles far larger trees than `/etc`.

choices.text: Because the registry is protected and `/etc` is not
choices.why: Both are protected. `/etc` needs root to write, as `/etc/shadow` showed.

choices.text: Because `/etc` is text files, and a change is a diff a person reads
choices.why: And every tool in lesson 8 works on it, which is the larger point.

choices.text: Because git was written on Linux and has support for it
choices.why: Git has no knowledge of `/etc`. It stores files, whatever they are.

prompt: Where does software you installed by hand belong, so the package manager leaves it alone?
hint: One of the ten entries in `/usr` exists for exactly this.

choices.text: `/opt/bin`
choices.why: `/opt` is a real answer for self-contained third-party software, but it is not the one paired with `/usr`.

choices.text: `/usr/local`
choices.why: Kept separate on purpose, so the two never fight over the same file.

choices.text: `/usr/bin`
choices.why: That is where the package manager puts things. Yours would be overwritten.

choices.text: `/home/you/bin`
choices.why: It works for one person, and nobody else on the machine gets it.

prompt: Fill the blank: logs live under ___, because that is where the machine writes things that change while it runs.
hint: Two directories deep, and the first is three letters.

prompt: In `/etc/passwd`, the second field of every line is `x`. What is it?
hint: It is not the password, and it has not been for decades.

choices.text: The account is disabled and refuses a login
choices.why: Disabled accounts are marked in other ways, and this `x` is on every line.

choices.text: The password, encrypted with a very old algorithm
choices.why: Nothing in this file is a password. That was true in the 1970s and is the reason it changed.

choices.text: A placeholder for a field nobody uses any more
choices.why: The field is very much in use. What changed is where the value is kept.

choices.text: A pointer: the real hash is in `/etc/shadow`
choices.why: Which is readable only by root, so that an ordinary user reading `/etc/passwd` learns nothing.

prompt: A machine with four people on it has twenty-six accounts. What are the other twenty-two for?
hint: Ask what else on the machine needs an identity.

choices.text: Accounts from people who left, kept for their files
choices.why: That happens, but it does not account for twenty-two of them.

choices.text: Programs — the web server, the database, the printing system
choices.why: So a flaw in one reaches only what that account may reach. The account is a blast radius.

choices.text: Groups, which are stored in the same file as users
choices.why: Groups are in `/etc/group`. This file holds users.

choices.text: Spare accounts the installer creates for future use
choices.why: Nothing creates accounts speculatively. Each one was added by something that needed it.

prompt: What makes root different from an account that has been given every permission?
hint: Ask what the kernel does at the moment of the check.

choices.text: Root belongs to each group on the machine
choices.why: It does not, and group membership would still be a check that runs.

choices.text: Root's permissions are recalculated at each login
choices.why: Nothing is recalculated. The difference is not in the permissions at all.

choices.text: For uid 0 the kernel skips the permission check
choices.why: Which is why there is no dialog, no confirmation and no undo.

choices.text: Root's home is outside the tree the checks apply to
choices.why: `/root` is an ordinary directory inside the same tree as everything else.

prompt: Fill the blank: the administrator's user id is ___, and that number is the whole of what makes it the administrator.
hint: A single digit.

prompt: What does a signed package index buy you that downloading an installer does not?
hint: Ask what you had actually verified in the second case.

choices.text: A faster download, because mirrors are closer
choices.why: Mirrors help with speed and are not what the signature is for.

choices.text: Software altered in transit refuses to install
choices.why: The check is cryptographic rather than a judgement about the website.

choices.text: A guarantee the software has no bugs in it
choices.why: A signature says who published it, not that it is correct.

choices.text: An automatic backup before anything is replaced
choices.why: Package managers do not snapshot your system. That is a separate tool.

prompt: Somebody's machine has been "up to date" for a year because they only ever run `apt update`. What were they missing?
hint: The two commands do two different jobs, and the names are unhelpful.

choices.text: `apt update` needs `sudo`, and they were running it as themselves
choices.why: Without `sudo` it would have failed loudly rather than appearing to work.

choices.text: They also had to reboot for the updates to apply
choices.why: Linux updates apply without a reboot, which is section 15's point.

choices.text: Their repository list was empty, so there was no index to fetch
choices.why: Then `apt update` would have reported nothing found, every time.

choices.text: `apt update` refreshes the catalogue; `apt upgrade` installs
choices.why: One reads the index, the other acts on it, and the naming catches everybody once.

prompt: Why is `curl -sSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` the line to be deliberate about?
hint: Ask what you get to inspect before anything executes.

choices.text: It downloads a script and runs it immediately, unsigned and unread
choices.why: You get no signature, no version, and no chance to read it first.

choices.text: `curl` is not installed by default on most distributions
choices.why: Whether it is installed is a detail, and easily fixed.

choices.text: It needs root, and asking for root is the risk
choices.why: That line frequently runs as an ordinary user, and is still the thing to watch.

choices.text: The software it installs resists being removed afterwards
choices.why: Removing it is awkward rather than impossible, and that is a smaller problem.

prompt: Which of these are true of installing from the distribution's repository? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four claims. Two are about what the package manager knows, one is about what it does not promise.

choices.text: Dependencies are resolved and fetched for you
choices.why: Working out what else is needed is most of what it does.

choices.text: Removing the package removes the files it put down
choices.why: It knows every one of them, because it put them there.

choices.text: Updating everything is one command
choices.why: Not one updater per program, each with its own schedule.

choices.text: The software is guaranteed to be the newest release
choices.why: A stable distribution deliberately ships older, tested versions. Lesson 2 is about that trade.

choices.text: A reboot applies the changes
choices.why: Files are replaced and services restarted. Only a kernel update genuinely needs one.

prompt: You opened `man ls` and now the terminal will not go back to a prompt. What do you press?
hint: It is a pager, and one letter leaves it.

choices.text: `Ctrl+C`
choices.why: It interrupts a running command, and the pager is not going to take the hint here.

choices.text: `Esc`
choices.why: It does nothing useful in a pager, and is the reflex people try second.
Which nobody tells beginners, and is the most common way to feel trapped in a terminal.

choices.text: `Ctrl+D`
choices.why: It ends input, and the pager is not reading any.

prompt: `man cd` disappoints. Why has `cd` no manual page of its own?
hint: Ask `type` what it is.

choices.text: It is too simple to have been documented
choices.why: Plenty of simpler programs have pages. That is not the reason.

choices.text: `cd` is part of bash, so there is no program to document
choices.why: `help cd` is where bash documents itself, and `type` is what tells you which kind of thing you have.

choices.text: The page exists but is in a section `man` does not search first
choices.why: There is no `cd` page in any section. There is no `/bin/cd`.

choices.text: Manual pages for builtins arrive with the developer tools
choices.why: No package adds one, because there is no separate program.

prompt: On a fresh container `man ls` prints a notice about the system having been minimized. What is the state of that machine?
hint: Section 04 warned about this shape of surprise.

choices.text: The manual is corrupted and should be reinstalled
choices.why: Nothing is corrupted. The pages were never put there.

choices.text: The command is missing its permissions to read `/usr/share`
choices.why: It would have said permission denied, which is a different message entirely.

choices.text: The image is broken and a different one should be pulled
choices.why: Every plain distribution image behaves this way.

choices.text: Normal — the image ships small, and `--help` works
choices.why: And the notice names the command that restores the pages, if you want them.

prompt: Match each question to the fastest way to ask it.
hint: One of them answers 'what kind of thing is this name', which is the odd one out.

pairs.right: `--help`

pairs.left: What does this one option mean, exactly?
pairs.right: `man`

pairs.left: Why is this command behaving oddly?
pairs.right: `type`

pairs.left: What is the command for doing X?
pairs.right: `apropos`

right_distractors: `history`, which lists what you have run
`file`, which reports what something is made of

prompt: `cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied`. How far did the line get before it failed?
hint: Work out which parts must already have succeeded for that message to exist.

choices.text: The shell could not find `cat`, so it stopped there
choices.why: `cat` is speaking. A program that did not run does not print its own name.

choices.text: `cat` ran, received the path, asked the kernel, and was refused
choices.why: Three things succeeded before the refusal, and the message says so if you read left to right.

choices.text: `cat` ran but did not receive the argument
choices.why: It printed the path, which is how you know it received it.

choices.text: The file does not exist, and this is how that is reported
choices.why: That has its own message, and it names the absence rather than the permission.

prompt: A command failed and `echo $?` prints 127. What happened?
hint: Two of the numbers belong to the shell rather than to any program.

choices.text: The program ran and reported a general failure
choices.why: That is 1, and it comes from the program itself.

choices.text: The program ran and refused one of its own flags
choices.why: That is usually 2, and the program says which flag.

choices.text: The shell could not find a command by that name
choices.why: 127 is the shell's own answer, and it means nothing was ever started.

choices.text: Somebody pressed Ctrl+C while it was running
choices.why: That is 130, which section 08 captured on screen.

prompt: `Permission denied`, and the section says not to reach for `sudo` first. Why not?
hint: Consider what else produces that message besides genuinely needing root.

choices.text: The refusal is a sign you are somewhere you did not mean to be
choices.why: Wrong directory, wrong copy — and `sudo` would have made that mess with authority.

choices.text: `sudo` does not work on files owned by root
choices.why: It very much does, which is most of what it is for.

choices.text: Running `sudo` is recorded, and the record counts against you
choices.why: It is recorded, and that is a feature rather than a penalty.

choices.text: The kernel refuses `sudo` on a second attempt at the same path
choices.why: Nothing tracks attempts like that.

prompt: Fill the blank: a command that worked leaves `$?` at ___, and the convention that anything else means failure is what lets lesson 9 write `a && b`.
hint: A single digit, and it is the only one that means success.

prompt: Which difference between Linux and Windows is a different idea rather than a different spelling?
hint: Ask which one changes what tools you can use.

choices.text: `/` against `\` as the path separator
choices.why: One character, two conventions. Everything else about a path is the same.

choices.text: `/home/you` against `C:\Users\you`
choices.why: The same idea with different names, as the table says.

choices.text: `.` for a hidden file against a hidden attribute
choices.why: Two mechanisms for one result, and neither changes what you can do.

choices.text: Configuration as text files against a binary registry
choices.why: Because `/etc` is text, every tool in lesson 8 administers the machine.

prompt: A file called `backup`, with no extension at all, runs when you type `./backup`. Why?
hint: Something in the mode decides, not something in the name.

choices.text: Linux guesses the type from the first line of the file
choices.why: The shebang chooses the interpreter for a script, and only after the system agreed to run it.

choices.text: Any file in your home directory may be run
choices.why: Where a file sits changes nothing about whether it runs.

choices.text: A permission bit says it may be executed
choices.why: The name is irrelevant, which is the mirror of `virus.exe` sitting in your home doing nothing.

choices.text: `./` in front makes the system run whatever follows
choices.why: `./` says where to look, not what may run.

prompt: What transfers from this course to a Windows machine? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate the ideas from the vocabulary, and remember what section 04 installed.

choices.text: The concepts: files, processes, permissions, users, services
choices.why: Both systems have all of them. You are learning a system, not a vocabulary.

choices.text: The commands, typed natively into PowerShell
choices.why: Lesson 10 gives the equivalents, and warns about the aliases that mislead.

choices.text: Everything, unchanged, inside WSL
choices.why: A real Linux beside Windows, which is why section 04 recommended it.

choices.text: The habit of reading an error from its first word
choices.why: It is a habit about paying attention, and it costs nothing anywhere.

prompt: Fill the blank: bash passes ___ between programs, and PowerShell passes objects — which is the difference lesson 10 treats as a real design choice rather than a flaw.
hint: One word, and it is what lesson 8 is entirely about.

prompt: You arrive on a machine you have never used. Which four questions do you ask first?
hint: Section 19 runs them in order.

choices.text: `ls`, `cat`, `file`, `head`
choices.why: Those look at things. First you establish where you are standing.

choices.text: `whoami`, `uname -s`, `pwd`, `ls -la`
choices.why: Who, what, where, and what is here — in that order, every time.

choices.text: `man`, `apropos`, `type`, `help`
choices.why: Those answer questions about commands, not about the machine.

choices.text: `id`, `sudo -l`, `passwd`, `groups`
choices.why: Those go deeper into your account, and lesson 4 is where they belong.

prompt: Match each message to the layer that produced it.
hint: Ask who would have had to be consulted for that sentence to exist.

pairs.right: The shell — it searched its path and found nothing
The kernel — it was asked, and refused

pairs.left: Text in the wrong place, colours stuck on
pairs.right: The terminal emulator — the drawing lost its place
The program — it ran, and rejected a flag of its own

right_distractors: The network, which dropped the connection
The package manager, which has not finished installing

prompt: Your terminal stops echoing anything you type. Before anything else, press:
hint: One key pauses output, and one resumes it.

choices.text: `Ctrl+C`
choices.why: It interrupts a running command. Nothing here is running.

choices.text: `Ctrl+D`
choices.why: It ends input, and would close your shell if it worked.

choices.text: `Ctrl+L`
choices.why: It clears the screen, which changes nothing about a paused one.

choices.text: `Ctrl+Q`
choices.why: Somebody reached for `Ctrl+S` to save, and this is the cure.

prompt: A file named `-report` will not open. Put the diagnosis in order.
items: The command fails with `invalid option`, naming a letter rather than the file
Recognise that anything starting with `-` is read as options
Put `--` before the name to say the options have finished
The command receives the name as an argument and opens it
trap: The common mistake is putting the quotes step in: quoting fixes a space, and does nothing for a leading hyphen — the shell was never the problem.

prompt: A script works when you run `bash script.sh` and fails with `cannot execute: required file not found` when you run `./script.sh`. What is it?
hint: One of those two paths reads the first line of the file.

choices.text: The script is not executable
choices.why: That refuses with `Permission denied`, and names the permission.

choices.text: The script is in a directory that is not on your path
choices.why: `./` says where to look, so the path is not involved.

choices.text: CRLF endings, so the shebang names `/bin/bash` plus a carriage return
choices.why: `bash script.sh` skips the shebang entirely, which is why only one of the two fails.

choices.text: The script calls a command that is not installed
choices.why: That would fail partway through, and after printing whatever came before.

prompt: Fill the blank: when a script behaves impossibly, run ___ on it — a CRLF file says so in the last clause of the answer.
hint: Four letters, and it reads bytes rather than drawing them.

prompt: Two files, `Config.yml` and `config.yml`, sit in one directory on a Linux server. What can you conclude?
hint: Ask what would have happened on a Mac.

choices.text: Two separate files, and one is probably a mistake
choices.why: Case matters here, so both were created — and a project that worked on a Mac now has one file too many.

choices.text: One is a link to the other
choices.why: A link is possible and would show differently in a long listing.

choices.text: The filesystem is misconfigured
choices.why: It is behaving exactly as a Linux filesystem does.

choices.text: One of them is hidden
choices.why: A hidden name begins with a dot, and neither of these does.

prompt: `echo $?` prints 130. What just happened?
hint: It is one of the two numbers that belong to the shell.

choices.text: A command was not found
choices.why: That is 127, and the shell says so in words as well.

choices.text: Somebody pressed Ctrl+C
choices.why: The exit status that means the program was interrupted.

choices.text: A command refused one of its flags
choices.why: Usually 2, and the program names the flag.

choices.text: The command succeeded
choices.why: Success is 0, and only 0.

prompt: You need to know which options a command you have never seen accepts, on a container with no manual pages. What do you run?
hint: One of the four ways to ask never depends on anything being installed.

choices.text: `man` the command, then install the pages when it fails
choices.why: A detour, when the answer is one keystroke away.

choices.text: `apropos` the command's name
choices.why: It searches manual descriptions, so on that machine it finds nothing.

choices.text: `type` the command
choices.why: It says what kind of thing the name is, not what options it takes.

choices.text: The command with `--help`
choices.why: Printed by the program itself, so it is there and never out of date.

prompt: A colleague says Linux and Windows differ only in naming. Which of these show otherwise? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four rows of section 18's table are ideas rather than spellings.

choices.text: Configuration is text, so `grep`, `diff` and git work on it
choices.why: A binary registry can be scripted, but not by the tools you already have.

choices.text: Programs pass text to each other, so small commands compose
choices.why: PowerShell answers the same problem with objects, which is a different idea rather than a different syntax.

choices.text: What makes a file run is a permission bit, not its name
choices.why: Which is why `virus.exe` in your home directory does nothing.

choices.text: Paths use `/` rather than `\`
choices.why: One character, two conventions, and nothing else about a path changes.

choices.text: Your documents are under a directory with your name on it
choices.why: `/home/you` against `C:\Users\you` is the same idea twice.

prompt: `ls /srv/data` prints nothing at all, and there is no error. What does that mean?
hint: Silence in a shell is not an error report.

choices.text: The directory does not exist
choices.why: That prints `No such file or directory`, and names the path.

choices.text: You do not have permission to read it
choices.why: That prints `Permission denied`, and names the path too.

choices.text: The directory is empty
choices.why: Nothing to list is nothing to print. Silence is success, which takes about a week to get used to.

choices.text: `ls` needs an option before it prints anything
choices.why: Plain `ls` prints names. It printed none because there were none.

prompt: A prompt ends in `#`. What should you do before pressing enter on anything destructive?
hint: The character is the warning.

choices.text: Notice you are root, and that nothing will confirm
choices.why: No dialog, no are-you-sure, no undo.

choices.text: Run `sudo` in front of the command to be sure it works
choices.why: You are already root. Adding `sudo` changes nothing.

choices.text: Check your internet connection
choices.why: Nothing about `#` has anything to do with a network.

choices.text: Type `exit` and start again as the same user
choices.why: Leaving is sometimes right, and it is not what the character is telling you.

prompt: You want to install a tool. Which option carries the least risk?
hint: Ask what was verified before anything ran.

choices.text: A `.deb` downloaded from the project's own website
choices.why: Better than a random one, and still unsigned by anybody your machine trusts.

choices.text: `sudo apt install`, from the distribution's repository
choices.why: Signed index, resolved dependencies, and a record of every file for removal later.

choices.text: `curl … | sh`, from the project's documentation
choices.why: Downloads a script and runs it immediately, unread and unsigned.

choices.text: Building it from source after cloning the repository
choices.why: Sometimes necessary, and it is the most work and the least checked.

prompt: Fill the blank: the command that tells you whether a name is a program, a shell builtin, an alias or a function is ___.
hint: Four letters, and section 16 recommends it before anything else when a command behaves oddly.
